_README.description: Master data file for the Chereskin Lab ADCP Data Portal. Edit this file to update all site content. Then run 'python3 -m http.server 8000' and open localhost:8000 to preview changes.
_README.image_paths: All image filenames in cruise.images[] are relative to the images/ folder. Example: 'nh9310_100_oa.jpg' → place file at images/nh9310_100_oa.jpg
_README.branding_note: project.logo, project.header_image and project.illustration_image are relative to the images/ folder (harvested from the original adcp.ucsd.edu under images/branding/). logo appears on the overview project card and the project page hero; header_image is the project hero banner photo (paired with header_credit); illustration_image sits beside the project page's Acknowledgments panel (paired with illustration_credit). All are optional — omit them to fall back to the plain card/hero layout.
_README.track_format: cruise.track is an optional array of [latitude, longitude] pairs used only when no measured track exists in the files listed under tracks_file.
_README.station_format: cruise.stations is an array of {lat, lon, label} objects for individual station markers on the map.
_README.ncei_url_note: cruise.ncei_url is the permanent NCEI accession landing page: https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/archive/accession/XXXXXXX . For 1999–2018 the JASADCP submissions were archived in batches, so many cruises share one accession; cruise.ncei_accession holds the bare number.
_README.contact: Chereskin Lab, Scripps Institution of Oceanography, UCSD
_README.tracks_file: data/drake_passage_tracks.json, data/calcofi_tracks.json and data/epac_tracks.json hold the measured ship tracks (ensembles with valid u and v) and the per-depth-bin data-coverage statistics extracted from the CODAS databases with pysadcp. A cruise is linked to its track through cruise.track_key, and cruise ids are unique across the projects, so the three files share one index. Regenerate them with make_drake_passage_web_tracks.py, make_calcofi_web_tracks.py and make_epac_web_tracks.py (kept outside this repository, they need pycurrents/CODAS and the raw loads). The Drake Passage file covers the 2019-onwards UHDAS loads, the 1999-2018 JAS-ADCP submissions and the NCEI accessions; the CalCOFI file covers the 1993-2009 JAS-ADCP submissions and the 2017-2023 UHDAS loads under uh_repo_ccs_dbs/, selected by select_calcofi_dbs.py; the Eastern Pacific file covers 22 JAS-ADCP submissions and 17 in-house loads spread over uh_repo, uh_repo_ccs_dbs and my_codas_proc, selected by select_epac_dbs.py.
_README.jasadcp_note: cruise.sac_id is the JASADCP (NODC/UH SAC) cruise id of the cruise's primary database, and cruise.jasadcp_url is its page at https://uhslc.soest.hawaii.edu/sadcp/DATABASE/<sac_id>.html . A cruise that submitted more than one sonar has one SAC id per database; they are all listed in cruise.sac_ids[] as {sac_id, sonar}, and the same ids appear per instrument in the tracks files.
_README.calcofi_selection_note: A CalCOFI cruise cannot be recognised from its CODAS metadata, and the California Current repositories hold plenty of neighbours (CCE-LTER process cruises, transits, other groups' work). The archived cruises come from JASADCP's own CalCOFI inventory, a copy of which is kept at input_info/harvest/jasadcp_calcofi_inventory.html; the 2017-onwards loads were identified against the CalCOFI program's cruise list by ship and date and are named explicitly in select_calcofi_dbs.py.
_README.webpy_gallery_files: data/antarctic_webpy_gallery.json and data/calcofi_webpy_gallery.json are the generated manifests for the CODAS section figures a cruise's Plots button selects. They are deliberately separate from cruise.images[]; make_drake_passage_web_gallery.py and make_calcofi_web_gallery.py (kept beside the CODAS science tools) render the databases offline into scratch and publish only static PNGs and thumbnails under images/antarctic-webpy/ and images/calcofi-webpy/. A cruise publishes one figure set per physical sonar over one shared set of section windows, so the columns of the gallery read against one another.
_README.plots_link_note: project.plots_link_label names the external plot page a cruise row links to beside its generated CODAS gallery. Set on the CalCOFI project as 'Atlas' because cruise.plots_url there is the 2008 CalCOFI ADCP Digital Atlas page of objectively mapped velocity, which the section figures do not replace. Left unset, an external plots_url is shown only for cruises with no generated gallery.
_README.calcofi_cruise_note: cruise.calcofi_cruise is the CalCOFI program's own name for the cruise (2107SR: year, month, ship), which is how CalCOFI indexes its hydrography and plankton data for the same stations.
_README.status_note: 'nav_only' marks a cruise whose navigation survives but whose CODAS velocity databases have not been located: it gets an illustrative cruise.track, no track_key and so no coverage drawer. It is deliberately not 'processed', which promises the data is available in house on request. Two Eastern Pacific cruises (TN265, TN310) are in this state.
_README.epac_select_note: The Eastern Pacific project is the eastern-Pacific part of the group's NASA submesoscale cruise list (input_info/Cryosat Accessions.xlsx) with the CalCOFI cruises removed, since those are their own tab. Membership cannot be decided geographically -- the same spreadsheet holds North Atlantic cruises and the repositories hold hundreds of unrelated neighbours -- so it is an explicit list in select_epac_dbs.py, checked against the committed archive inventory rows in input_info/harvest/jasadcp_epac_inventory.txt. The cruise rows are generated by tools/build_epac_cruises.py. NCEI accessions come from input_info/harvest/epac_ncei_accessions.csv, which records for each cruise which accession the portal links and how the data reached the archive.

projects.vessel: ARSV Laurence M. Gould & RVIB Nathaniel B. Palmer
projects.illustration_credit: LMG ADCP program sticker, Chereskin Lab
projects.description: The Antarctic Circumpolar Current (ACC)  is the largest current on the planet. As the narrowest land gap on its  circumpolar path, Drake Passage is an ideal monitoring spot. The NSF-funded Drake Passage time series collected shipboard ADCP observations from 1998 to 2024 during all transits of Drake Passage and on cruises to the Antarctic Peninsula made by the supply vessel for Palmer Station. A primary goal was to obtain a long time series at near-repeat locations to unambiguously separate temporal from spatial variability and short-term variability from long-term trends. The time series comprises 455 transects of upper ocean currents from a NB150 ADCP (profiling depths 22 m to 250 m) and 309 transects from an OS38 ADCP (profiling depths 46 m to 950 m). These transects have been used to study the ACC on time scales from seasonal to interannual and on space scales from eddies to jets.
projects.project_description: The ACC is the largest current on the planet. It plays a key role in the Earth system connecting all the world’s oceans. As the narrowest land gap on its  circumpolar path, Drake Passage is an ideal monitoring spot. However, it is also one of the windiest and roughest stretches of water on the globe. The only ship that crosses Drake Passage year-round is the supply vessel for Palmer Station. The ACC comprises multiple velocity jets that flow west to east around Antarctica and form a  barrier that separates warmer waters to the north from colder waters to the south. Ocean eddies break through the ACC barrier, transferring heat across the ACC towards Antarctica. When warmer ocean waters intrude onto the Antarctic continental shelf, they contribute to glacial melt and ice shelf retreat. Over the past several decades the Southern Ocean has warmed and winds have increased. Somewhat surprisingly, the Drake Passage ADCP observations show that the ACC, though pushed by faster winds, has not accelerated (Gutierrez et al., Nature Comms 2024); a faster current would present a stronger barrier to heat transfer. Instead, ocean eddies have increased in the region between the northernmost ACC fronts in Drake Passage. Combining concurrent temperature and velocity observations from the time series has provided a better understanding of heat transfer across the ACC by eddies (Gutierrez et al., JPO 2020). Additionally, the time series has provided valuable measurements to resolve the coastal circulation of the Antarctic Peninsula (e.g., Savidge and Amft, DSR 2009) as well as ground-truth for satellite measurements and numerical model predictions covering the entire ACC.
projects.methods_text: Data processed using CODAS3 with standard heading calibration procedures. Bottom tracking was available for shallow transits near the Peninsula. Navigation corrections applied via differential GPS.

projects.vessel: NOAA Ship Bell M. Shimada, NOAA Ship David Starr Jordan, R/V New Horizon, R/V Oceanus, NOAA Ship Reuben Lasker, R/V Roger Revelle, R/V Sally Ride

projects.description: Three decades of shipboard ADCP measurements of upper-ocean currents off southern and central California, made on the quarterly cruises of the California Cooperative Oceanic Fisheries Investigations (CalCOFI).
projects.project_description: CalCOFI has occupied the same station grid off southern California since 1949, and since 1993 the Chereskin Lab has measured the currents over it with a shipboard ADCP. The quarterly cruises trace the California Current, the eastern limb of the North Pacific subtropical gyre, as it carries cool, fresh subarctic water equatorward past the coast, together with the poleward California Undercurrent beneath it and the eddies and filaments that carry water offshore. Because the grid is reoccupied four times a year on fixed lines, the velocity sections stack into a record long enough to separate the seasonal cycle from interannual signals — the 1997–98 El Niño, the warm anomaly of 2014–16 — and to be read alongside the hydrography, nutrients and plankton the same stations have collected for seventy years. The first decade of the record, 1993–2004, was mapped objectively to velocity streamfunctions consistent with geostrophy and published as the CalCOFI ADCP Digital Atlas (Chereskin and Trunnell, 1996; Chereskin, 2008); the 2017-onwards cruises are processed in house and carry up to three sonars each, reaching past 1,000 m where the 38 kHz Ocean Surveyor is fitted.
projects.methods_text: The 1993–2009 cruises were measured with a hull-mounted RDI 150 kHz narrowband ADCP and processed with CODAS3; all forty were submitted to the Joint Archive for Shipboard ADCP and are archived at NOAA/NCEI. Objective mapping was applied to the 1993–2004 cruises to produce velocity streamfunctions consistent with geostrophy, which is what the CalCOFI ADCP Digital Atlas publishes at 50 m and 100 m. The 2017-onwards cruises were logged with UHDAS and processed with CODAS in house: an Ocean Surveyor 75 kHz on the NOAA ships, and an Ocean Surveyor 38 kHz, an Ocean Surveyor 150 kHz and a Workhorse 300 kHz together on R/V Sally Ride, the three sonars covering the water column from about 10 m to beyond 1,000 m.

projects.name: Eastern Pacific — submesoscale process cruises
projects.vessel: R/V Atlantis, R/V Ka'imikai-o-Kanaloa, R/V Kilo Moana, R/V Marcus G. Langseth, R/V Melville, R/V Oceanus, R/V Point Sur, R/V Roger Revelle, NOAA Ship Ronald H. Brown, R/V Sally Ride, R/V Sikuliaq, R/V Thomas G. Thompson
projects.description: Shipboard ADCP measurements of upper-ocean currents from cruises across the eastern Pacific in both hemispheres, processed under the NASA Ocean Surface Topography Science Team to examine submesoscale processes. The series reaches from the Chilean and Peruvian margins and the equatorial line to the California Current and the Oregon and Washington shelf, and includes the long transits that connect them.
projects.project_description: Submesoscale motions — fronts, filaments and eddies a few kilometres across — sit at the limit of what satellite altimetry can resolve, and shipboard ADCP sections are one of the few ways to measure them directly over a wide range of dynamical regimes. The cruises gathered here were processed together for that purpose: rather than one programme repeating one station grid, they are an opportunity sample of eastern Pacific cruises whose underway velocity data was reprocessed to a common standard. They span 54°S to 49°N and the eastern-boundary upwelling systems, the equatorial current system and the open subtropical gyre. The work was carried out for the NASA Ocean Surface Topography Science Team (OSTST) under awards NNX17AH53G and 80NSSC21K1822.
projects.methods_text: All cruises were processed with CODAS3 under UHDAS or its predecessors, with standard heading and phase calibration. Most carry more than one sonar — an Ocean Surveyor in both ping modes, often with a 300 kHz Workhorse alongside — and every database the cruise published is reported separately, so the depth reach and data return of each instrument can be read on its own. Twenty-two of the cruises were submitted to the Joint Archive for Shipboard ADCP and carry SAC ids; the rest were processed in house.
projects.acknowledgments: These data were collected aboard many vessels and processed by the Chereskin Lab at Scripps Institution of Oceanography, UCSD, and by the University of Hawaii Currents Group, with support from the NASA Ocean Surface Topography Science Team under awards NNX17AH53G and 80NSSC21K1822. The archived cruises were submitted through the Joint Archive for Shipboard ADCP, a collaboration of NOAA and the University of Hawaii Currents Group.
